transcript: Well, the federal government needs to act and we need to act accomplished. College athletics is incredibly important. It unifies us. It brings us together. It has provided an avenue for thousands upon thousands of young men and young women to get an excellent education and team work and discipline. And it unifies communities. It ties alums and fans to their schools. College athletics is a magical institution and I think it is in real jeopardy right now. The current state of affairs is the Wild West when you combine unlimited NIL rights with an unlimited transport portal. We are entering an arena where every player goes to the highest bidder and the loyalties of players to teams and the ethos of college sports is in real jeopardy. We're also at risk of seeing a handful of giant mega schools with all the money, creating super teams and the rest of schools unable to compete, which I think would be terrible. To have college athletics succeed, you have to have some monocum of parity. Part of what's beautiful about college athletics is on any given day, even a small school can win. And that's something that I think is in real jeopardy right now. I believe Congress needs to act. I think there should be a national standard. There have been multiple bills introduced in Congress. I introduced legislation that was the product of spending many months listening to stakeholders, listening to universities, listening to conferences, listening to the NCAA, listening to players, and trying to really solicit best practices that the legislation I've introduced. Number one protects NIL rights for college athletes. I think that is fair and I think it's right that if you worked incredibly hard, if you've developed remarkable skills, you ought to be able to enjoy the fruits of your labor. And so I think it is a much more fair system that college athletes who have extraordinary talent should be able to reap the rewards from that. But at the same time, there needs to be a set of rules and a set of standards across the board. And my legislation empowers the NCAA to set those rules. There are different bills that have been filed that would create a governmental agency or a quasi-governmental agency to set those rules. I think that's the mistake. I think the last thing anyone should want is elected politicians deciding what constitutes pass interference. That would be a nightmare. The NCAA has its faults to be sure. But I think it is far better to have a governance system where the member institutions have a say and it is drawn from the stakeholders. And so my hope is that the recent settlement, the House settlement for the NCAA will provide an impetus for Congress to step in and act. In order for Congress to act, there's got to be bipartisan agreement. We're not there yet, but I'm hopeful we'll get there.
